title: To Lam heads to Australia – but Vietnam still won’t pick a side
gist: Australia and Vietnam are converging out of shared uncertainty about the great powers rather than shared strategy, with two-way goods trade passing $30 billion in 2025 and a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership since 2024. The author stresses the limits: Australia backs a forward US military presence and AUKUS while Hanoi is alliance-averse and will keep prioritising China — and only 31% of Australians now trust the US to act responsibly, barely above the 28% who trust China.

themes.theme: Middle-power convergence born of US unreliability

insights.claim: Australia and Vietnam are drawing closer not out of shared strategy but shared uncertainty about the great powers, as the United States rejects the multilateral and rules-based order it helped create and leaves allies seeking alternatives.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Middle-power hedging pacts are a fragile substitute for alliance structure — they diversify but do not deter, so regional risk premia stay elevated.
insights.quote: Australia and Vietnam are drawing closer not out of shared strategy but shared uncertainty about the great powers.
insights.locator: To Lam heads to Australia – but Vietnam still won’t pick a side

insights.claim: Both Australia and Vietnam want to preserve a stable balance of power in the Pacific and prevent any single power dominating the region, but their views and interests diverge in notable ways.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Shared objective, incompatible methods — expect economic and people-to-people depth in the relationship but little hard security integration.
insights.quote: Both countries want to preserve (Opens in new window) a stable balance of power in the Pacific and prevent the emergence of any single power (Opens in new window) dominating the region. But their views and interests diverge in notable ways.
insights.locator: Faced with an unreliable United States

insights.claim: Since becoming General Secretary in 2024, To Lam has considerably expanded Hanoi's diversification strategy, making his first trip to China as a signal of commitment to Vietnam's most important partner before travelling to the United States for the UN General Assembly the following month.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Sequencing is the signal in Vietnamese diplomacy — China first confirms Beijing retains structural priority regardless of Western outreach.
insights.quote: His first trip was to China, a signal of his commitment to Vietnam’s most important partner.
insights.locator: Since assuming the top leadership position

insights.claim: To Lam has made three trips to Laos and two to Cambodia, indicating the weight Vietnam places on its mainland Southeast Asian neighbours relative to more distant partners.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Vietnam's continental Southeast Asian bloc is an underappreciated sphere of influence — relevant to Mekong infrastructure and cross-border energy projects.
insights.quote: He has also made three trips to Laos and two to Cambodia
insights.locator: Since assuming the top leadership position

insights.claim: To Lam attended the inaugural meeting of US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace in Washington in February 2026, then travelled to China, India, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka and Thailand between April and June.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Six major capitals in three months quantifies the diversification push — a leading indicator of Vietnamese trade and investment agreements to follow.
insights.quote: Between April and June, To Lam went to China, India, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka, and Thailand.
insights.locator: In February 2026, To Lam visited Washington

insights.claim: Hanoi has hosted an unusually broad set of visiting leaders including Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Vietnam is a rare venue receiving both Xi and Putin alongside US allies — a bellwether for who retains access in Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: Hanoi has also hosted numerous heads of state

insights.claim: Australia supports an active forward US military presence, has relied on the United States as its security guarantor for more than half a century, and has invested billions in the AUKUS nuclear submarine technology-sharing pact with the United Kingdom and United States despite regional and domestic pushback.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: AUKUS is the structural obstacle to deeper Australia-Vietnam security ties — Hanoi will keep the relationship economic to avoid being read as aligning.
insights.quote: It has invested billions in a nuclear submarine technology sharing pact with the United Kingdom and United States, AUKUS, which has encountered regional (Opens in new window) and domestic pushback
insights.locator: Australia supports an active forward US military presence

insights.claim: Vietnam's elevation of ties with Australia is an instance of its multidirectional foreign policy aimed at strategic autonomy: Hanoi is averse to alliances and will continue to prioritise its relationship with China, with whom it shares a border and a complicated history.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Do not read Vietnamese partnership upgrades as bloc alignment — Vietnam will absorb Western capital while refusing security commitments.
insights.quote: Hanoi is averse to alliances and will continue to prioritise its relationship with China, with whom it shares a border and a complicated history.
insights.locator: Vietnam has elevated ties with Australia

themes.theme: Australian public trust collapse in both superpowers

insights.claim: Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in global affairs according to the latest Lowy Poll — a historically low figure roughly on par with the 28% who express confidence in China.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Near-parity in trust between ally and strategic competitor erodes the domestic political base for AUKUS-scale spending — a medium-term risk to the program.
insights.quote: only 31% (Opens in new window) trust the United States to act responsibly in global affairs, according to the latest Lowy Poll

insights.claim: Australians express nearly identical levels of trust in Donald Trump (21%) and Xi Jinping (20%), even as a majority continues to support the alliance with the United States.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: The gap between institutional alliance support and leader-level distrust is where policy volatility originates — watch it if a US demand becomes politically costly.
insights.quote: Australians express similar levels of trust in Donald Trump (21%) and Xi Jinping (20%).

insights.claim: Two-way Australia–Vietnam goods trade surpassed $30 billion in 2025, meeting a growth target set during Anthony Albanese's 2023 visit to Hanoi, with Vietnam Australia's 10th largest goods trading partner and Australia Vietnam's seventh largest.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: The bilateral trade target was hit on schedule — a credible base for the next tranche of commitments at the To Lam visit.
insights.quote: Two-way trade in goods surpassed $30 billion (Opens in new window) in 2025, meeting a growth target (Opens in new window) set during Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s visit to Hanoi in 2023.
insights.locator: Vietnam is Australia’s 10th largest trading partner

insights.claim: The two governments have agreed to double bilateral investment, which stood at US$1.9 billion as of December 2025 — a small base relative to the $30 billion trade flow.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Investment is an order of magnitude below trade, marking the capital channel as the growth area and the likely deliverable of the visit.
insights.quote: The two sides have also agreed to double (Opens in new window) bilateral investment, which stood at US$1.9 billion (Opens in new window) as of December 2025.
insights.locator: The two sides have also agreed to double

insights.claim: Australia has committed resources to Vietnam's green energy transition and pledged nearly $100 million in development aid to Vietnam this year.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Australian aid is being routed into Vietnamese energy transition projects — a channel for Australian renewables and grid contractors.
insights.quote: pledged nearly $100 million (Opens in new window) in development aid to Vietnam this year

insights.claim: Roughly 327,000 Vietnamese-born people lived in Australia in 2025 with more than 36,000 Vietnamese students studying there, Vietnamese is Australia's fourth most commonly spoken language, and Vietnam is the ninth most popular destination for Australian tourists.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Education and diaspora flows are a durable revenue channel for Australian universities and a stabiliser insulating the relationship from geopolitical swings.
insights.quote: Vietnamese is the fourth most commonly spoken language in Australia.

insights.claim: The Australia–Vietnam partnership is likely to grow in importance as the Labor government continues to prioritise Canberra's engagement with Southeast Asia and the Pacific, with To Lam's first visit to Australia set to signal the relationship's direction.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Southeast Asia engagement is a standing Labor priority — expect continued aid, trade and education deals irrespective of the US-China cycle.
insights.quote: the Australia-Vietnam partnership is likely to grow in importance
insights.locator: To Lam’s visit – his first to Australia
